subject: Computing
source: National Curriculum KS2 Computing (safe, respectful and responsible use of technology; collecting, analysing and presenting data); links forward to the Year 7 Computing Overview in the school's Drive

lessons.title: Digital footprint and strong passwords
objectives: Explain what a digital footprint is and how it is made
Describe what makes a password strong
Make decisions about what is safe to share online

keywords.def: the trail of information about you left online
a secret code that proves it is really you
choices that control who can see your information

starter: Bismillah. Name three pieces of personal information you should keep private.
What would you do if a stranger sent you a message online?
Is everything you post online gone when you delete it? What do you think?

teach.heading: Your digital footprint
bullets: Photos, comments and likes leave a trail.
Some of it stays online for a long time.
Others can copy and share it.
teach.note: Use the footprints in sand analogy: you leave marks as you walk. Ask what footprints they might have left already (a game username, a school website photo). Misconception: 'delete means gone'; screenshots and copies may remain.

teach.heading: Think before you post
bullets: Would I be happy if my family saw it?
teach.note: Connect to adab: the Prophet (peace be upon him) said that whoever believes in Allah and the Last Day should speak good or remain silent (Bukhari and Muslim). Apply this to typing as well as speaking. Run quick scenarios and ask pupils to decide: post or not?

teach.heading: Strong passwords
bullets: Never share it except with a parent.
teach.note: Compare 'ahmed2014' with 'purple-tractor-sandwich'. Explain why the second is stronger: it is longer and not guessable from personal information. Do not ask pupils to share their real passwords at any point.

teach.heading: Privacy settings
bullets: Only accept people you know in real life.
Ask a trusted adult for help.
teach.note: Remind pupils that most social media platforms have a minimum age (often 13). Note that the settings differ by app; the principle is to limit who sees information. Encourage a family conversation.

practice: Which is the stronger password: 'mohammed10' or 'green-lamp-river-hat'? Explain why.
Should you post a photo showing your school badge and street name? Why not?
Give one example of a digital footprint you leave when playing an online game.
independent: Design a poster 'Five rules for a safe digital footprint' with a rule for each of: posting, passwords, sharing photos, privacy settings, telling an adult.
Create three strong passwords from random words, but do not use them for any real account.
Write a short script for what you would say to a younger sibling who wants to post their address on a gaming chat.
exit: Give two features of a strong password.
lessons.homework: With a parent or carer, check the privacy settings on one app or game you use at home. Tell the class one change you made.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a sorting activity with pictures of safe/unsafe posts and a password checklist. Stretch: explain how a company might use data from a person's footprint.

lessons.title: Respect online: unkind behaviour and how to report it
objectives: Recognise unkind or unacceptable behaviour online
Describe ways to respond and report concerns
Explain how to be a good digital citizen

keywords.def: bullying using phones, games or the internet
tell a trusted adult or use a report button

starter: Bismillah. What is a digital footprint?
Give an example of a kind online message.
Why is it harder to see how someone feels when we type than when we speak?

teach.heading: What is cyberbullying?
bullets: Leaving someone out of a group chat.
Sharing secrets or photos without permission.
teach.note: Handle sensitively; do not ask pupils to share personal experiences in front of the class. Use fictional characters (Ali and Sara). Explain that bullying online can follow someone home and be seen by many people.

teach.heading: Our adab
bullets: Allah tells us not to mock others.
Not to call people hurtful nicknames.
teach.note: Surah al-Hujurat (49:11) tells believers not to ridicule each other and not to insult or call each other offensive nicknames. State it plainly, in your own words, then relate it to the internet: the same adab applies in chat, games and comments.

teach.heading: What can I do?
bullets: Do not reply or fight back.
Save the evidence: take a screenshot.
Block the person and use report buttons.
teach.note: Teach these four steps and practise them as a chant: do not reply, save, block, tell. Mention that in the UK, Childline (0800 1111) is a free, confidential helpline for children. Make sure pupils know a named trusted adult at school and at home.

teach.heading: Be an upstander
bullets: Do not join in or share unkind posts.
Support the person who is hurt.
Tell an adult if you see it.
teach.note: Define bystander and upstander. Role-play a group chat where one pupil is being teased; ask what a good friend would do. Link to the idea of helping someone who is wronged, as a part of good character.

practice: Ali's friends took a funny photo of him and shared it without asking. Is that okay? What could Ali do?
Put the steps in order: tell a trusted adult, take a screenshot, do not reply, block the person.
Give a kind message you could send to a classmate who is being left out.
independent: Write a short comic strip showing a pupil who receives an unkind message and uses the four steps.
Write three rules for a kind class group chat.
List three trusted adults you could go to, and explain why you chose them.
exit: Name one thing you should do if someone sends you an unkind message.
What is the difference between a bystander and an upstander?
lessons.homework: Talk with a parent or carer about what you would do if you saw something unkind online, and write down your plan in three steps.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide the four-step chant as a visual card and role-play instead of writing. Stretch: discuss why people sometimes behave unkindly online when they would not in person.

lessons.title: Collecting data and using a spreadsheet
objectives: Plan a simple survey and collect data
Enter data into a spreadsheet using rows and columns
Use a formula to calculate a total

keywords.def: facts and figures that can be collected and studied
a grid of cells for storing and working out data
one box in a spreadsheet, such as B2
an instruction in a cell to calculate something

starter: Bismillah. What does 'report' mean when we talk about online safety?
How could you find out which fruit is the class favourite?
What is a table? Draw one in the air with your hands.

teach.heading: Collecting data
bullets: Record each answer with a tally.
teach.note: Choose a question: What is your favourite fruit: dates, mango, banana or grapes? Run a quick poll in the chat using hands up or emojis. Record a tally on screen. Ask why choices help (they make data easier to count).

teach.heading: Spreadsheet layout
bullets: A cell is named by both: B3.
teach.note: Open a spreadsheet and enter Fruit in A1 and Votes in B1. Enter the poll data. Ask pupils which cell contains the votes for mango. Misconception: pupils write the number before the letter; the letter comes first.

teach.heading: Formulas
bullets: The total changes if data changes.
teach.note: Type =SUM(B2:B5) in B6. Change one vote and show the total updating. Explain that spreadsheets calculate for us. Link back to variables: the cell holds a value that can change.

teach.heading: Keep data accurate
bullets: Save the file with a good name.
teach.note: Talk about the amanah (trust) of recording data accurately: if we record results, they should be honest and careful. Show an example with a typing mistake (a 50 instead of a 5) and how it changes the total.

practice: Which cell is in column C, row 4? (C4)
A spreadsheet shows dates 6, mango 9, banana 4, grapes 5. Write a formula to add the votes if they are in B2 to B5. (=SUM(B2:B5))
What is the total number of votes? (24)
independent: Create a survey question with four choices and collect answers from 10 people (family or class).
Enter the data in a spreadsheet with headings and use SUM to find the total.
Write one sentence saying what the data shows.
exit: What does a formula always start with?
Which cell is in column B, row 2?
lessons.homework: Ask 10 people in your family or friends which season they like best and record the answers in a table.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a spreadsheet already set up with headings and colour-coded cells. Stretch: use =AVERAGE or =MAX on a column of numbers.

lessons.title: Charts: presenting and explaining data
objectives: Create a bar chart from spreadsheet data
Label a chart with a title and axes
Write a conclusion that matches the data

keywords.def: a chart with bars whose height shows how many
the horizontal or vertical line of a chart

starter: Bismillah. What is a cell reference? Give an example.
Which formula adds cells A1 to A5? (=SUM(A1:A5))
Which is easier to read: a list of numbers or a picture? Why?

teach.heading: Why use charts?
bullets: A good chart is clear and labelled.
teach.note: Show the same data as a table and as a bar chart. Ask which one shows the favourite fruit fastest. Explain that charts present data in a form people understand quickly.

teach.heading: Making a bar chart
teach.note: Demonstrate in the spreadsheet. Highlight A1:B5, then insert a chart. Point out that the categories go on the horizontal axis and the counts on the vertical axis.

teach.heading: Label your chart
teach.note: Compare an unlabelled chart with a labelled one. Ask what is missing from the first one. Misconception: pupils skip labels because they know their own data; others do not.

teach.heading: Write a conclusion
bullets: Mango was the most popular fruit.
Use numbers to back it up.
teach.note: Model a conclusion sentence: 'Mango was the most popular with 9 votes, and bananas were the least popular with 4 votes.' Encourage pupils to use numbers from the chart and to be honest about what the data shows, not what they hoped it would show.

practice: Which axis shows the categories (fruits) in a column chart? (horizontal)
Write a title for a chart about favourite seasons.
A bar for summer is 12 tall and a bar for winter is 5 tall. Which season is more popular? By how much? (summer, by 7)
independent: Turn your survey data from last lesson into a bar chart with a title and labelled axes.
Write a 2-sentence conclusion using numbers from the chart.
Swap with a partner and give feedback using: what is clear, what could be clearer.
exit: What three things should every chart have?
Write a conclusion for a chart showing 10 votes for football and 4 for cricket.
lessons.homework: Find a chart in a newspaper, app or website and say what it shows in two sentences.
lessons.send: SEND/EAL: provide a chart template with title and axes already labelled to complete. Stretch: compare a bar chart with a pictogram and explain which is better for the data.
